title: Encapsulation, access modifiers and immutability
body: Access modifiers decide who can use a member. `public`: anyone. `private`: only the containing type (the default for members). `protected`: the type and its derived types. `internal`: any code in the same assembly (the default for top-level types). `protected internal` and `private protected` combine these. `file` (C# 11) limits a type to its source file.

Encapsulation means callers can change an object only through members that keep its invariants. A `BankAccount` with a public `Balance` setter cannot guarantee the balance never goes negative; one with a private setter and a `Withdraw` method that checks the amount can.

`readonly` fields can be assigned only in their declaration or a constructor. `const` values are compile-time constants baked into callers, so changing a public const requires recompiling every consumer; prefer `static readonly` for values that might change between versions.

Exposing a mutable collection breaks encapsulation even when the property is get-only: callers can still add or remove items. Return `IReadOnlyList<T>` (or a copy) and keep the `List<T>` private. Note that a read-only view is not a frozen copy; it reflects later internal changes.

Immutability makes objects easier to share across threads and to reason about. Before adding a setter or a public field, check which invariant could be broken through it and whether a method with validation, `init` or a new object would serve better.
challenge: Write a Counter class whose Value can only increase through Increment(int by) that rejects non-positive amounts by returning false. Show one accepted and one rejected call.
question: A class exposes `public List<string> Items { get; }`. What can callers still do?
correct: Add and remove items through the returned list
wrong: Nothing; get-only makes the list immutable
Only read items, because the setter is missing
reasoning: get-only stops callers replacing the reference, not mutating the object it refers to.
